1:
"At that time" has to be pinned down, and the three who try disagree about how much can be pinned. Gill reports Aben Ezra placing it on the fortieth day and Jarchi at the end of forty days, and rules out the first forty on the ground that those days ended with the giving of the tables Moses broke; the order here belongs to the second forty, after he had fallen before the Lord and entreated him, and comes as a token that God was reconciled. Ellicott sorts the commands rather than the days. The order to make an ark had been given in the earlier period; the order to hew the tables came after Moses had seen the glory of God from the cleft in the rock, but before the forty days of intercession, which followed this command rather than preceding it. Calvin declines the whole enterprise. Moses is relating more fully what he had already mentioned in an inverted order of time, and the notice about the ark stands out of its proper place, since the ark belonged to the tabernacle. It is exacting too much, he says, to require that things related together be referred to the same instant of time.

Who made the ark is the harder question, since Moses says he made it and the account of the tabernacle assigns it to Bezaleel. Henry offers two ways out: that Bezaleel afterwards finished and overlaid with gold what Moses had begun as a plain chest of shittim-wood, or that Moses is said to make it because, going up the second time, he ordered it made against his coming down. Either way he thinks the ordering of it early was deliberate, an earnest to the congregation that the tables should not miscarry a second time as they had the first. Ellicott reports and rejects a sharper solution. Rashi supposed two arks, one to go out to war and one to stay in the tabernacle; there is no foundation for it, though Ellicott allows that a temporary receptacle may have been made to hold the tables until Bezaleel's was finished, as a temporary tent had served before the tabernacle was built. Henry turns the vessel into a figure before leaving it: Christ is the ark in which our salvation is now kept safe, so that it may not be lost as it was in the first Adam, who held it in his own hand.

Henry makes the hewing itself instructive. The tables that were first written were broken because Israel had broken the commandments, and God might justly have broken the covenant too; that they were renewed when his anger turned away he takes as the surest evidence of reconciliation. That Moses must cut the stone while God does the writing he reads as an order of operations in grace — the law prepares a heart by conviction and humiliation, but only grace then writes the law upon it. On the second tables he notices what is not there. The ten commandments were ten words, not ten volumes; the second edition needed neither correction nor amendment, and what God wrote did not differ from what he had spoken, from which Henry concludes that the written word is as truly God's word as anything spoken to the prophets. He hears Moses point toward the sanctuary at the last clause — there they be — and turns it on his own hearers: God has entrusted us with Bibles and sabbaths and sacraments, and there they be; we lodge them with you. Gill adds only that the order followed the intercession, and came as the token that reconciliation had been granted.
2:
Ellicott begins by correcting a common error — that Moses wrote the law the second time. It arises, he explains, from a change of person in the Exodus narrative, where the same pronoun refers first to Moses and then to the Lord; the hewing was Moses's work, the writing God's. Gill makes the same division and draws two inferences from it. That the words were the very same, without alteration or variation, shows their authenticity, since they were of God and not of Moses; and it shows their invariableness, no change having been made in them though the people had broken them, of which the breaking of the tables was itself a representation. Wesley reads the renewal as evidence: the tables were broken because Israel broke the commandment, and their being written again proves that God's wrath was turned away. Keil and Delitzsch put the same thing in terms of what was owed — the grace of God turned toward the people once more through the intercession of Moses.

From that division Ellicott builds a figure and carries it a long way. The tables of stone stand for the fleshy tables of the heart, on Paul's authority; the first pair answer to the heart of Adam, which came fresh from its Maker's hand with the word of the law written on it and then perished by the fall at the foot of the mountain of the law. The humanity that ascended to receive the Spirit for us was prepared by the Mediator on earth, and the second man received a new covenant that is not letter but Spirit, putting God's laws in men's minds and writing them on their hearts. On that reading the ark and the tabernacle which received the law become a figure of God's human temple and of the renewed heart. Gill stays with the carpentry, noting only that Moses ordered the chest and Bezaleel made it, of the same shittim wood as the ark that afterwards stood in the holy of holies.

Two smaller notes close the section. On "the day of the assembly" Ellicott suggests the New Testament equivalent would be the day of the Church, and sets the two Pentecosts side by side — the one on which the letter was given, and the one on which came the Spirit that gives life — remarking that each aspect of the covenant produced a Church after its kind. On the last clause he warns the English reader against the pluperfect. Hebrew has none, and the tense of a verb is settled by its context rather than its form, so "the ark which I had made" should be simply "which I made," which may well mean caused to be made and refers to the ark Bezaleel built under direction. The closing words are better rendered as a statement that the tables remained there. Gill notices the small gesture the verse begins with, that Moses turned himself away from the Lord, out of whose hands he had just received them.
6:
These verses interrupt the argument, and everyone says so. Wesley calls the little history a plain parenthesis, closed when Moses returns to his subject four verses later, and reads it as evidence that the prayers were answered: they went forward under God's guidance, and though Aaron died on the way, the breach was made up when Eleazar came in his place. Calvin agrees about the purpose and denies any intention of a full itinerary — Moses is not listing stations as the complete catalogue in Numbers does, but marking where Aaron died. In that death the people might recognise the punishment of their own rebellion, while the substitution of the son was a sign of God's fatherly grace, and became the standing rule of succession in that family. Gill is less content. If the first place named is the one generally supposed, Israel had already made a great many journeys and encampments before reaching it; and since Aaron died at the very next station, that was thirty-eight years after they left Sinai. It is hard to say, he admits, what reason there can be for mentioning these two or three journeys just here.

Clarke prints Kennicott's remarks on the passage, and they put the difficulty at its sharpest. These verses, Kennicott argues, not only have no connection with what stands before and after them, but as they read in the present Hebrew text they contradict that text directly. Here Israel journeys from Bene-jaakan to Mosera; the complete catalogue of the march has them going from Moseroth to Bene-jaakan. Here Aaron dies at Mosera; there he dies on Mount Hor, the seventh station further on. Here the route runs Bene-jaakan, Mosera, Gudgodah, Jotbath; there it runs Moseroth, Bene-jaakan, Hor-hagidgad, Jotbathah. And even if the marches could stand as they are, he asks, what possible connection is there between arriving at Jotbath and the separation of the tribe of Levi? His own solution is textual: the difficulties, he says, are happily removed by the Samaritan Pentateuch, which reads the passage differently and closes it with a fresh paragraph about turning northward from Seir. Clarke will not endorse the reconstruction but will not have it dismissed either, adding only that these remarks should not be hastily rejected.

The others prefer to relieve the pressure rather than emend. Keil and Delitzsch fasten on the phrase "at that time," and deny that it points to the year of Aaron's death — which is where Knobel had found his contradiction with the other books. It refers quite generally, they hold, to the time Moses is speaking of throughout this passage, namely the restoration of the covenant at Sinai, so that the separation of Levi is dated there and not later. Calvin makes the same move without the polemic, observing that in this discourse the order of the history is simply inverted, since Moses places the setting apart of the Levites after Aaron's death. On the place-names themselves Gill reports the division among the Jewish commentators: Jarchi identifies Gudgodah with Hor-hagidgad, as most do, while Aben Ezra denies the identification and takes it for a general name covering Zalmonah, Punon and Oboth, the stations reached after Mount Hor. Calvin allows the same latitude, suggesting either that the places bore more than one name or that Israel passed through the well-watered valley without pitching camp there.
8:
The separation of Levi is dated by nobody in quite the same way. Ellicott places it at Sinai, after Moses came down the second time, and not at Aaron's death — though he notices that the two events rhyme, since both the dying priest and the set-apart tribe lose a territorial inheritance through bearing the burden of the law. Gill dates it later still, after the tabernacle was erected, and suggests that what stands here may be a renewal of the separation, or a repetition prompted by the mention of Eleazar's succession. Wesley softens the phrase to "about that time," referring it to the descent from the mount. Calvin is less interested in the date than in the authority: the point of rehearsing the history is that nobody should attempt in pride to overthrow God's inviolable decree, so Moses testifies that the dignity of the tribe has God for its author, and the words "unto this day" look back over the instances in which that favour had been shown, lest any similar rivalry should arise again.

The three duties named in the verse have been used against the book itself, and Ellicott answers the charge. A recent critic, he reports, held that the writer of Deuteronomy knows no distinction between priests and Levites; Ellicott prefers Rashi's note, which distributes the clauses — bearing the ark belongs to the Levites, standing before the Lord to minister and blessing in his name to the priests. Wesley glosses the middle phrase from its use elsewhere, noting that standing before the Lord is said of prophets and of angels alike, being the posture of a minister; and he defines the blessing as the performance of those holy services and the giving of those instructions to which God's blessing was promised, done in his name because done by his commission. Keil and Delitzsch treat the whole appointment as a manifestation of mercy toward Israel rather than a privilege granted to a family, and connect it with the earlier election of Aaron and his sons to the priesthood.

On the compensation for having no inheritance, Gill gives the practical reason from Jarchi — a tribe kept at the service of the sanctuary had no leisure to plough and sow — while Wesley identifies the portion concretely as the tithes and offerings which belong to God and are assigned by him to the Levites for their subsistence from generation to generation. Ellicott hears the phrase against the immediate context and lets it stay personal: the Lord was the inheritance of Levi as he had just been the inheritance of Aaron, whom he had lately taken to himself. The section closes where it began. Gill reads the forty days of the second stay as matching the first in length and in fasting, and takes the command to move as the visible answer to the intercession: God not only forgave the people but ordered Moses to go before them toward the land. Ellicott quotes Rashi to the same effect, that though they had turned aside and erred in the matter of the calf, the word came, Go, lead the people. Wesley finds a type in it, that the one who had saved them by his intercession should also have the conduct and command of them.
12:
Henry hears an orator opening his peroration. Moses turns on his hearers with a question, and Henry answers it with another from the Psalms — what shall I render? — since when we have received mercy from God it becomes us to enquire what returns we shall make. He adds that the question is safe to ask, because what God requires turns out to be nothing but what is highly reasonable in itself and of unspeakable advantage to those required. Gill names the mercies that prompt it: forgiveness, a fresh intimation that they should possess the land, and the renewal of the promise made to their fathers. Wesley says the same in half a line, that the requirement comes by way of duty and gratitude for such amazing mercies. Ellicott quotes Rashi in the same key — though ye have done all this, his affection is still set upon you, and after all your sin he asks nothing of you but to fear — and reports the rabbinic maxim drawn from the verse, that everything is in Heaven's hand to bestow except the fear of Heaven. He will not leave the maxim standing alone, and sets against it the promise to put that fear into men's hearts.

Both Henry and Clarke break the demand into its clauses, and the two lists differ instructively in temper. Clarke's is compact and four-fold: fear him as the God who made, preserves and governs you; walk in all his ways, not in your own nor in those of the people of the land; love him, having confidence in him as father and friend and loving him in return for his love; and serve him with all the heart, meaning the whole of the affections, and all the soul, meaning the will, understanding and judgment. Henry's runs longer and distinguishes the two affections at the root of the rest — fear him as a great God and our Lord, love him as a good God and our Father — before adding the walking, the serving, the keeping of the statutes, the honouring of his name in an oath, and the cleaving to him that follows from having chosen him. On the keeping of statutes he adds the point Clarke leaves implicit, that obedience is not merely rewarded but is itself the better condition: to be meek and humble, chaste and sober, just and charitable, patient and contented is what makes a man easy and safe and truly great.

Calvin uses the verse as the place to state what the whole law comes to. Paul had given its true end as charity out of a pure heart and a good conscience and faith unfeigned, against interpreters who had turned aside to vain jangling; and as the law stands on two tables, so it reduces to two heads, that we love God with all the heart and our neighbour as ourselves. Moses does not unite the two in one passage, but Christ, by whose Spirit he spoke, has done it for him, answering that the second commandment is like the first. From this Calvin draws a short definition — that nothing is required for a good life except piety and justice. He anticipates two objections. Paul appears to add a third term when he bids us live soberly as well as righteously and godly, but soberness is the seasoning of a just and pious life rather than a third ingredient, since no one proves that he aims at holiness except by living chastely and temperately. And where a passage names only the love of neighbour, religion is not being buried but tested, since it is the way of hypocrites to cover themselves with ceremonies as with a mask of sanctity.
14:
Gill and Wesley divide the phrase in the ordinary way — the airy and starry heaven first, then the third heaven, called the heaven of heavens for its eminence, the seat of the divine Majesty and the dwelling of angels and glorified saints. Clarke is not satisfied with that. All the words in the original are plural, he observes, and to say that the first means the atmosphere, the second the planetary system and the third the region of the blessed is to explain very little. He takes them rather for a statement of the sheer immensity of the creation, in which we may conceive one system of heavenly bodies, and others beyond them, and others again in endless progression through the whole vortex of space — every star in the vast abyss of nature being a sun with its own numerous attendant worlds, so that there may be systems of systems in endless gradation up to the throne of God.

Keil and Delitzsch read the doubled phrase as deliberately exhaustive: by the heavens of the heavens the idea of heaven is used up entirely, nothing being left outside it. The point of exhausting it is the contrast that follows — this God, who might as easily have chosen any other nation, or indeed all the nations together, directed his special love to Israel alone. Calvin puts the same comparison of the great with the small more warmly. It was inestimable condescension that God should in a manner pass by heaven and earth, with all their beauty and abundance, and set his heart on a few obscure men. He presses the Hebrew of the next clause too, which says literally that the Lord coveted to love their fathers, a word marking not a decision but an inclination of feeling; Jerome's rendering, that God adhered to them, he thinks has not caught it.

On what grounded the choice, all four are agreed and each says it once. Calvin insists that Israel differed from other nations neither by personal dignity nor by excellence of race, but only because it pleased God to prefer them while ruling equally over all; and he notes that the love is said to reach not the fathers only but their descendants in their persons, or the exhortation that follows would not fit. Ellicott compresses it to a sentence — the whole world belongs to the Lord, and for all that he chose thy fathers above all people. Wesley denies any prior obligation: all being equally his creatures, the choice of these out of and above the others proceeded only from God's good pleasure. Gill grants the same and adds what followed from it, the particular expressions of love shown in acts of kindness done to the fathers and promises made to them.
16:
Circumcision of the heart is taken by all of them as the point of the outward rite rather than a metaphor added to it. Clarke calls the command a plain proof from God himself that the precept always pointed at spiritual things, the object never having been the cutting away of flesh but the purification of the soul, without which forms and ceremonies avail nothing; loving God with all the heart, the heart being circumcised so that it can, was from the beginning the end and fulfilment of the whole law. Calvin traces the same sense from the rite's original purpose — a solemn consecration by which the children of Abraham were initiated into the worship of God and separated from the heathen, administered in infancy so that the visible sign might teach that the defilements of flesh and world were to be renounced. Ellicott gives the verse its Pauline form, that circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit and not in the letter, and notes that the Hebrew reads as promise rather than command in its second half: circumcise the foreskin of your heart, and ye will harden your neck no more.

Keil and Delitzsch define the thing negatively — laying aside all insensibility of heart to impressions from the love of God — and state the dependence flatly: without circumcision of heart, true fear of God and true love of God are alike impossible. Gill raises the difficulty that follows from calling it God's own work, and answers it: the exhortation is made in order to bring men to a sense of their need of it and of its importance, and so to stir them up to seek it from the God who alone can perform it. Wesley presses the figure itself, that the foreskin stands for the filthiness which, if not cut away, leaves a man profane and unclean in God's sight. Calvin adds the reciprocity the passage assumes. Having known God to be so gracious by experience, the people owe him a returning love, and nothing could be baser than to withhold the testimony of a pious life; the command to be stiff-necked no more is at once a demand and a reproof for the obstinacy in which they had too long hardened themselves.

The titles that follow are the ground of the demand, and the commentators fasten on the turn the passage takes. Ellicott quotes Rashi's exclamation — behold his might, and close beside his might thou mayest find his humility — and matches it with the psalm that sets the healing of the broken-hearted next to the numbering of the stars. Clarke dwells on the power alone, taking God of gods to mean the source whence all being and power proceed, so that every agent but himself is finite and he may counteract or suspend or destroy any action whatever. Calvin explains why the argument turns to the fatherless and the stranger. We injure the abject the more wantonly because they seem altogether deserted; but God, who accepts no man's person, is not deterred by their poverty from succouring them, and one who sits so high has respect to the lowly. Wesley draws the warning for Israel out of the same impartiality — since God deals equally with all sorts of men, they must not flatter themselves that he will bear with their sins because of his kindness to their fathers. Gill and Keil both take the love of the stranger as the test of whether the heart has in fact been circumcised.
20:
Keil and Delitzsch read the four verbs as one thing shown three ways: reverence for God appearing in deed, where he is served; in the heart, where he is cleaved to; and with the mouth, where his name is sworn by. Gill takes the first of them as the widest, fear including the whole worship of God, external and internal alike; Wesley glosses the third as cleaving with firm confidence, true affection and constant obedience. Ellicott notices that the clause returned in the wilderness temptation as our Lord's last answer, and that the Hebrew word-order carries an emphasis the English loses — Jehovah thy God shalt thou fear, him shalt thou serve, and to him shalt thou cleave. He quotes Rashi for the sequence: only after all these qualities are established in a man does the permission to swear by God's name follow, since only then would the name not be profaned in the swearing.

Calvin takes up the oath from the side of what an oath can do to God. Since he is eternal and immutable truth, he cannot be more grossly insulted than by being summoned as a witness to a falsehood, which Calvin calls a shameful and wicked pollution. He notes that covetousness is what usually drives a man to it, so that greed for gain makes the rapacious not only defraud their neighbours but grow insolent toward God himself; a prohibition aimed at protecting men from injury turns out to be aimed at religion as well. He observes that the heathen never saw this. They professed to reverence the divine name in their oaths and yet made no scruple of deceiving where they judged the other party to deserve it, as the poet's Thyestes boasts that he never pledged faith to a faithless man, and thought a villain's treachery released him.

"He is thy praise" is read by Gill as meaning the object and matter of it, God deserving the praise of all his creatures for his perfections and his works. Calvin turns the phrase round and reads it as a warning. God is called the praise of his people because he is their honour and their ornament, so that they have nothing to boast of outside him; take this glory away and nothing would remain to them but ignominy and shame, which is why it would be perverse beyond anything to refuse the Creator when he freely offers himself as their God. Keil and Delitzsch supply the ground of the praise from the following clause, taking the terrible things to be acts of omnipotence that fill men with trembling at the majesty of the Almighty. Clarke turns it on the reader instead: it is an eternal honour to any soul to be in the friendship of God, and strange that those who fear him should be ashamed to own it while sinners proclaim their relationship to Satan boldly enough.
22:
The chapter closes on an arithmetic that Clarke finds staggering and Ellicott finds worth defending. Gill fixes the number first: the seventy who went down were seventy in all, Jacob and his sons included and not additional to them. Clarke sets against it the six hundred thousand of the census, and adds the detail that gives the comparison its edge — all of those had themselves died in the forty years, save three men, so that the multitude standing before Moses was another generation again. From this he draws not a calculation but a moral: how easily God can increase and multiply, and how easily diminish and bring low, since with unlimited power he can do whatever he will, and will do whatever is right.

Ellicott takes the difficulty head on. He grants that the increase of Israel within the time the narrative allows presents a problem, and answers it first from the character of the event, since Scripture consistently presents the multiplication as the fulfilment of a divine promise and not as a purely natural process. But he refuses to rest the case there, and turns to the genealogies in the first book of Chronicles, where the line of Judah discloses a very extensive multiplication, much of it falling inside the years of the sojourn in Egypt; the family of Hezron he singles out particularly. His decisive instance is a descendant of Simeon of whom it is written that he had sixteen sons and six daughters, while his brethren had not many children, neither did all their family multiply like the children of Judah. Modern calculations, Ellicott concludes drily, are perhaps not quite adequate to deal with a rate of increase like that.

Gill closes where the promise began, noting that the Lord had made them as the stars of heaven for multitude exactly as he had said he would, so that the verse is offered less as a statistic than as a discharged undertaking. The three readings converge on that point from different directions. Clarke reads the growth as a display of power that could as easily be reversed; Ellicott reads it as a promise being kept through means that were partly ordinary and partly not; Gill reads it as the plain correspondence of the event to the word given to Abraham. What none of them does is treat the number as a difficulty to be explained away, and Ellicott is explicit that the marvel is meant to be felt rather than reduced.
